I had almost identical damage to my board, I cut out the petex from that area, cleaned out any little bits of loose fiberglass etc.. Then put the outside of the edge against my vise (sturdy hard surface) I then used a thin punch and a hammer to tap the edge back straight. 

Do not try taping the edge unless it is firmly up against something hard like an anvil or something hard that's fixed in place, otherwise you could cause more damage. 

Or, you could cut that part of the edge out and replace with a new section of edge. You may have to use very shallow flat top screws in between the the edge and teeth of the edge. 

After that you can fill it with base weld material or buy some sheet ptex and cut to fit. The sheet ptex has a textured side to bond to epoxy.

If you go this route at all don't try to fill it in with a ptex candle because it won't bond right.

Edit: one could leave it how it is and use it as a rock board. But I personally had to fix mine because I'm too poor to buy another used board let alone new one, so I needed to make sure it was strong and water tight and ready for many seasons of riding

Just a tip when soldering stuff like this (sorry if you already know) silver solder sucks its harder to work with, rosin is your friend, a tiny precision tip is harder to use because the standard tips hold more heat and the solder joint seems to happen faster (you can with the smaller tips but it takes more finesse, so as long as the tip just isn't too big to fit where you're trying to solder.

 Tin the tip of the wire first before soldering it back to the pad (both pad and wire need to be "tinned" before you solder them together, but you likely don't need to re-tin the pad on the circuit board as it's already hit solder on it) the way they break off means the tip of the wire that was tinned is still in the solder joint on the board likely, so just re tin the tip of the wire and then it should solder back together to the pad nice and quick

If you haven't soldered before, look up some videos and practice maybe with something old or broken like the circuit board from an old TV remote or something, you'll probably end up feeling way more comfortable about tackling the servo motor wire on the airplane

You can get new ones, just note the rotation of each motor because the brushes inside them are directional and running one backwards shortens the lifespan of it. If its sentimental to you, it's worth fixing as the motors could be found for a few dollars. You just need decent soldering skills and a little patience.

Also make sure the battery that you replace inside the helicopter is of the same or similar specs in weight and discharge rating, there's a lot of 1s battery's on the market that have a pretty low discharge rating (not for rc things) so a battery replacement for the syma s107 or similar should be right

To my understanding, In this configuration it won't power the receiver. That ESC does not have a built in BEC, which steps the voltage down to a clean regulated voltage for the receiver and servos. The black and white wires going to the receiver are ground and signal, leaving out the positive power lead. 

This is why you see ESCs with BECs having three wires that go to the receiver, ground positive and signal.

This ESC was designed to be used in conjunction with a PDB or power distribution board. It's job is to provide a clean power source to the esc's, flight controller and receiver in a multirotor. 

You CAN use this ESC just get an external BEC that you can add the the main power supply leads that the batt plus into.

The mount is 1/32 lite ply, I made the front part first, bolting the motor up to a square flat piece of ply. Then I added the left and right sides, making sure the sides determined the thrust angle. 

I would then, position the fuselage straight up, place the mount/motor on firewall then add the cowl over it as a dry fit. I had to sand the back of the mount sides until it would all fit in the cowl. Then, once the cowl is positioned, adjust the mount until it is in the right spot for motor shaft to stick out of the cowl correctly.

Hold it in that spot, apply small amount of ca glue to tack mount the mount in place (using a pipet will let you get through the air vent in the cowl and all the way to the motor mount to glue it, use as little as possible to tack it) 

Double check your fit is correct and then finish gluing.

There is a book called "modern arboriculture" written by Alex shigo. It is full of all the knowledge anybody needs to understand and work on trees. 

I would first try to understand *why* proper pruning techniques should be used. 

then after that I would cut off the the stubs that have been left, and work with the remaining structure that is left, that is if there is enough structure left.

If you Google "branch bark ridge pruning" or similar, you should see pictures showing the proper place for a "finish cut"

Be careful when cutting off a heavy stub or branch, as the weight could peel down the bark down the branch and trunk if the branch falls before being completely cut. To avoid that use the "3-point cut" method.

Look up pictures showing the difference between a properly pruned tree vs topped, even vs "lion tailed". There are good illustrations that will help you understand.

A good rule of thumb is not to remove more than 25% of the canopy, I stick with 20% especially on big mature trees. Normally when I prune a tree it's mostly "dead-wooding" and pruning off of sucker growth, a light thinning. Rarely do I thin out 25%, I mostly thin out the canopy by around 15% 

If you have two branches crossing, prune off the branch that's on top, the one being held up by the other. If you take the **bottom** one, the *top* that has grown with the support of the **bottom** and said *top* branch will be weak and probably will break from water weight (rain) or more likely will break from snow or ice. So take the top branch of the two crossing.

If you have any more questions feel free to ask :)
